name: Retool
tagline: Build one internal CRUD tool over a trusted database with role-aware actions

pricing.notes: Advertised annual-equivalent Team price; monthly billing is higher.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Up to 5 users; 500 workflow runs/month; 5 GB storage; 20 agent hours; 250 AI credits
tiers.notes: Builder and internal-user roles are free inside the 5-user cap.

tiers.name: Team, builder
tiers.limits: Builder seat; 5,000 workflow runs/month per organization; 1,000 pooled AI credits after introductory bonus
tiers.notes: Official US page exposed the annual-equivalent price; monthly amount was not stable in the crawl.

tiers.name: Team, internal user
tiers.limits: Internal end-user seat; shares the organization's workflow and AI allowances

tiers.name: Business, builder
tiers.limits: Builder seat; 5,000 workflow runs/month; 3,000 pooled AI credits; advanced permissions and environments

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom builder/internal/external users, support, security and deployment terms

pricing.freeTierCaps: 5 total users; 500 workflow runs/month; 5 GB storage; 20 agent hours; 250 AI credits
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; published self-serve figures are role-based per user
pricing.hiddenCosts: Builder and internal-user seats have different rates; extra workflow capacity costs $75 per 5,000 runs, AI credits are pooled and reset without rollover, Agents are metered separately, and external-user pricing changes after the included band

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Retool, build one internal CRUD tool over a trusted database with role-aware actions. The hard boundary is connectors, component library, permissions, workflows, and hosted runtime, plus connectors, runtime reliability, and governance.
coreLoopDIY: Define tables and views, build one internal CRUD tool with role-aware actions over one approved trusted database, and deploy it for a small trusted team.
requirements: API credentials for one selected integration
whatYouLose: connectors, component library, permissions, workflows, and hosted runtime
ongoingBurden: schema migration, auth, permissions, connector drift, queues, deployments, backups, and auditability
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Retool because the builder is only useful when its runtime, connectors, permissions, and deployments remain boring for years. The recurring cost buys schema migration, auth, permissions, connector drift, queues, deployments, backups, and auditability, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Appsmith
priorArt.desc: Large open-source low-code platform for internal applications and data sources.

alternatives.name: Appsmith Free
alternatives.desc: Five people can build and run database-backed internal apps in the hosted product without paying.

facts.install: Hosted signup for Appsmith Cloud Free
facts.engines: Appsmith's AI/agent features use Appsmith-managed AI services; exact model availability is product-controlled rather than a local backend
facts.dataFormat: App definitions, users, and secrets live in Appsmith Cloud; connected business data remains in the source database/API, while query results pass through Appsmith
facts.gapVsPaid: Appsmith's hosted free product has a smaller connector, component, mobile, debugging, and production-observability surface than Retool.

alternatives.name: Budibase
alternatives.desc: Internal apps, forms, automations, and portals in one box; much closer to Knack than its developer branding suggests.

facts.install: Docker image or Docker Compose; Kubernetes is also supported
facts.engines: Model-agnostic; the agent builder supports bring-your-own AI provider credentials
facts.dataFormat: Built-in app data and app definitions are stored in CouchDB, files in MinIO/S3-compatible object storage, and connected external data remains in its source system
facts.gapVsPaid: Budibase is faster for standard CRUD but gives up Retool's fine-grained UI composition, custom-code flexibility, connector breadth, and debugging tools.
facts.setupBlocker: Requires Docker and persistent storage; production use also means owning upgrades, TLS, backups, and database/network access

alternatives.name: Directus Self-Hosted
alternatives.desc: A polished data studio with tables, forms, dashboards, flows, and APIs; free only below its organization-size ceiling.

facts.install: Docker Compose with SQLite for a test install, or a supported SQL database and persistent file storage for production
facts.engines: Optional AI Assistant supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints with the operator's API key
facts.dataFormat: Business records stay in the connected SQL database; assets live in configured local or object storage; Directus metadata is stored alongside the database
facts.gapVsPaid: Directus is a polished data studio around a database, not a general arbitrary internal-app canvas, so bespoke multi-source tools require much more custom work.
facts.setupBlocker: Requires Docker, a secret, persistent database/uploads, backups, TLS, and attention to Directus's non-OSI license and free-tier limits

alternatives.name: Retool Free
alternatives.desc: The same product is enough for one small team: five users, unlimited apps, every database and API connector, and role-aware actions.

facts.engines: Retool-managed AI models and agents; Free includes pooled AI credits and limited agent hours, while bring-your-own model keys are plan-dependent
facts.dataFormat: App definitions, Retool Database rows, and Retool file storage live in Retool Cloud; connected source data remains in the user's databases/APIs, although query results transit Retool
facts.gapVsPaid: It is the same product under user, workflow, AI, governance, and support limits that become restrictive as soon as the internal tool serves more than a tiny team.

alternatives.name: ToolJet Free
alternatives.desc: Two builders, 50 users, two apps, and the actual database and API connectors, not a screenshot-only trial.

facts.install: Hosted signup for ToolJet Cloud Free
facts.engines: ToolJet AI uses vendor-hosted AI services and plan credits; bring-your-own LLM keys are an Enterprise add-on
facts.dataFormat: App metadata, ToolJet Database tables, secrets, and files live in ToolJet Cloud; connected source records remain in their external database/API
facts.gapVsPaid: ToolJet's component and connector ecosystem, debugging experience, mobile tooling, and production polish are less mature than Retool's.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Team plan and a small-team internal app DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Retool in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: define tables and views, build one internal CRUD tool with role-aware actions over one approved trusted database, and deploy it for a small trusted team.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create a schema editor for text, number, boolean, date, enum, and relation fields.
Generate list, detail, create, edit, and kanban views from the schema.
Implement role-based read and write rules for admin and member roles.
Support one REST connector with encrypted credentials and explicit field mapping.
Add an activity log, CSV import or export, backups, and health checks.
Ship Docker Compose with migrations and a seeded example workspace.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out arbitrary user-authored code execution.
Deliberately leave out a broad integration marketplace.
Deliberately leave out native mobile binaries and enterprise compliance.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
